title: Continued Fractions of Square Roots
short: When d is not a perfect square, √d has a repeating continued fraction, and its convergents are the best rational approximations: no fraction with a smaller denominator comes closer.
trouble: Students switch to rounded decimals, which hides the repeating pattern. Keep exact expressions such as 1/(√7 − 2) and rationalize.

blocks.html: A rational number has a finite continued fraction. An irrational number does not: the algorithm runs forever. For square roots something remarkable happens: the partial quotients repeat. Finding the pattern needs exact arithmetic with radicals, the kind practiced in Algebra 1.
The algorithm. Start with $x_0 = x$. At each step take the whole part $a_k = \lfloor x_k \rfloor$, then flip what is left: $x_{k+1} = \dfrac{1}{x_k - a_k}$. Then $x = [a_0; a_1, a_2, \dots]$.

Theorem (Lagrange). If $d$ is a positive integer that is not a perfect square, the continued fraction of $\sqrt{d}$ is periodic: $$\sqrt{d} = [a_0; \overline{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{r-1}, 2a_0}],$$ where the bar marks the block that repeats forever, and the block always ends with $2a_0$.

Each $x_k$ can be written exactly as $\dfrac{\sqrt{d} + m}{c}$ with whole numbers $m$ and $c$, by rationalizing the denominator each time. One can show $0 \le m < \sqrt{d}$ and $0 < c < 2\sqrt{d}$, so there are only finitely many possible pairs $(m, c)$. Sooner or later a pair repeats, and from then on every step repeats too. Rounding to decimals destroys exactly this information, which is why the computation must stay exact.

blocks.name: nt-euclid
blocks.cap: The $\sqrt{7} \times 1$ rectangle cut into squares never comes out even, but the counts settle into the block 1, 1, 1, 4. The last column, $p^{2} - 7q^{2}$, is always small: a hint of Pell's equation.

blocks.title: The simplest case
steps: $x_1 - 2 = \sqrt{2} - 1$, the same leftover as before, so every later quotient is 2.

blocks.title: Best approximations
blocks.q: Find the convergents of $\sqrt{7} = [2; 1, 1, 1, 4, \dots]$ up to $\frac{p_4}{q_4}$.
steps: $\frac{37}{14} \approx 2.642857$, while $\sqrt{7} \approx 2.645751$. No fraction with denominator at most 14 comes closer.

blocks.html: Switching to rounded decimals. With $\sqrt{7} \approx 2.6458$, a few flips amplify the rounding error until the quotients come out wrong, and the repeating pattern is never seen. Keep exact forms such as $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{7} - 2}$ and rationalize: multiply top and bottom by $\sqrt{7} + 2$.
For $\sqrt{d}$, flip and take whole parts with exact radicals: $\sqrt{d} = [a_0; \overline{a_1, \dots, 2a_0}]$ is periodic, and its convergents are the best rational approximations to $\sqrt{d}$.
